Bulk Segregant Analysis

The aim of the analysis is to determine the variants that are related to chill coma recovery time (CCRT) phenotype. Four pools were used for the analysis: * Tolerant parental line pool: BKK12 * Sensitive parental line pool: BKK13 * Extremely tolerant offspring pool: CCRT < 30 minutes * Extremely sensitive offspring pool: CCRT > 60 minutes

100 females for each of the parental pools were collected from F2 generation. For extreme phenotype offspring pools, the virgin females of F2 generation were collected and kept at rearing temperature on standard corn molasses medium until they were 4-6 days old. The single flies were transferred into empty vials and placed on ice for 3 hours to induce chill coma. Then, the vials were placed back to the rearing temperature for recovery. The flies that were able to stand in the first 30 minutes were collected as extremely-fast-recovering offspring. The flies that were able to stand in the second 30 minutes were discarded. At the end of the third and the last 30 minutes, the alive flies were collected as the extremely-slow-recovering offspring regardless of their recovery state. The chill coma recovery assay was repeated until 100 flies were collected for each offspring pool.

The flies were placed into 1.5mL eppendorf tubes in groups of 10 and snap-frozen in liquid nitrogen for DNA extraction. The DNA was extracted using MasterPure™ DNA Purification Kit (Epicentre, Madison, WI, USA). The DNA samples were pooled together and sent for whole genome sequencing to an external facility (Novogene, Cambridge, UK), which performed high-throughput sequencing using a Novaseq 6000 sequencer (Illumina, San Diego, CA, USA) to generate 150-bp paired-end reads. On average 62.4 million reads were generated per sample.

The raw data was mapped to Drosophila ananassae genome (NCBI Drosophila ananassae Annotation Release 102) using the Burrows-Wheeler Aligner tool (version 0.5.0). Further processing -sorting, merging, duplicate removing- was done using samtools (version 1.18). Variant calling was performed using freebayes (version 1.3.8). The variants were filtered using bcftools (version 1.18). Finally, GATK-VariantsToTable tool was used to prepare the data for further analysis on R (version 4.2.2).

Import Data

We import the .table files that contain the variants of each pool. These files were generated using GATK VariantsToTable tool. The headers of columns are:

  1. CHROM

  2. POS

  3. REF

  4. ALT

  5. QUAL

  6. DP

  7. TolerantOffspring.GT

  8. TolerantOffspring.AD

  9. TolerantOffspring.DP

  10. TolerantOffspring.GQ -> this one we do not need and therefore removed from the table.

We also import the tables that include the ortologous gene list and the REFSEQ numbers that correspond the FlyBase numbers.

After removing the unwanted column, we combine the desired sample pools together. For parental comparison, we combine the tolerant (fast-recovering) and sensitive (slow-recovering) parental pools. For offspring comparison, we combine all the pools together, because the further analysis takes the parental differences into consideration and explains the main differences between the two extreme phenotypes.

We save the new data frames into a new file with .table extension to be able to use it with importFromGATK() function

Analysis

Now we perform

  • the QTL analysis and generate the plots for “No of SNPs in 1Mb window” and “delta-SNP index”
    • SNP index (∆SNP) refers to the subtraction of the alternate allele frequency value of the low bulk from the high bulk (∆SNP)
  • the G’ analysis and generate the associated plots
    • G-statistics takes advantage of a log-likelihood statistic LOD between allele frequencies

SNPset - all pools

Now, we can obtain the significant regions associated with the trait. These regions are significantly different between the extreme-phenotype offsprings.

Annotation

For the gene information of the significant regions, we use the genome annotation provided with the reference genome. To find the gene names in the given significant regions, we first simplify the data. We need the sequence names, starting position, and the final position of the significant region.

Using makeGRangesFromDataFrame(), findOverlaps(), and annotation[subjectHits()] functions, we identify the genes in the significant regions. For further analysis (i.e. GO analysis), the D. melanogaster orthologs are used.
